## 4 eras of NLP

### Era 1: Symbolic era

*1950s–1970s*

**Complex, hard-coded rules written by linguists.**

Alan Turing's ["Computing Machinery and Intelligence"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_Machinery_and_Intelligence) (1950), IBM's Russian to English translations (1954), and MIT's [ELIZA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ELIZA) (1964–1967), the first rule-based chatbot.

### Era 2: Lexical search

*1980s–1990s*

**Statistical methods.**

Algorithms learn patterns & probabilities from data (large corpora).

### Era 3: Dense retrieval

*2000s–2010s*

**Machine learning & early deep learning models.**

Vector embeddings, e.g. [Word2Vec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2Vec) (2013): mathematical representation of words based on their semantic meanings & contextual relationships.

[Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurrent_neural_network) such as [Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_short-term_memory) networks for speech recognition & translation.

### Era 4: LLMs

*2017–present*

**Transformer-based large language models.**

Self-attention mechanism, massive scaling, generative AI.

[BERT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BERT_(language_model)), [GPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Products_and_applications_of_OpenAI#Text_generation), [Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_(language_model)), [Claude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_(AI)), [Kimi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimi_(AI)), [GLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLM_(AI)), [Llama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llama_(language_model)), etc.

## The question

:::{.emph}

If LLMs can do everything, are task-specific methods dead?

Let's find out with one test case.

:::

### Benchmark: BEIR/SciFact

The [SciFact](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14974) [@wadden2020factfictionverifyingscientific] dataset is a benchmark for scientific claim verification (2020), part of the [BEIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663) [@thakur2021beir] standard suite of information retrieval benchmarks:

- [5,183 scientific abstracts]{.emph},
- [1,409 scientific claims]{.emph},
- [Expert annotators' ground truth]{.emph}.

### Get the data

```{.bash}
curl -L -o scifact.zip \
  https://public.ukp.informatik.tu-darmstadt.de/thakur/BEIR/datasets/scifact.zip
```

:::{.notenoit}

Alternative methods to get the data:

- from the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/allenai/scifact),
- from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/scifact):

```{.python}
from datasets import load_dataset
dataset = load_dataset("allenai/scifact")
```

:::

### Structure of the data

[scifact.zip]{.codelike} unzips to a [scifact]{.codelike} dir with:

[corpus.jsonl]{.codelike}: a corpus of research abstracts \
  ➔ `_id`, `title`, `text` (abstract of scientific paper).

[queries.jsonl]{.codelike}: scientific claims to be verified against the corpus \
  ➔ `id`, `text` (claim), `label` (`contradict` / `support`).

[qrels]{.codelike} dir with [train.tsv]{.codelike} & [test.tsv]{.codelike}: relevance judgments for training & testing \
  ➔ `corpus-id`, `query-id`, `score`.

### Metric: nDCG@10

[Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discounted_cumulative_gain) at rank 10 is a standard ranking quality metric in information retrieval, search engines & recommendation systems.

Measures how well a system places the most relevant items within the first 10 results.

```{.python}
def ndcg_at_k(ranked, qrels, k=10):
    dcg = sum(qrels.get(d, 0) / np.log2(r + 2)
              for r, d in enumerate(ranked[:k]))
    ideal = sorted(qrels.values(), reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(g / np.log2(r + 2) for r, g in enumerate(ideal))
    return dcg / idcg if idcg else 0.0
```

### Scores in context

Across the 18 datasets of BEIR, BM25 averages an nDCG@10 of 0.48 [@thakur2021beir].

SciFact is one of the most keyword-friendly datasets of the suite: scientific claims are full of rare exact terms.

:::{.note}

Rule of thumb on this benchmark: 0.70+ is strong & 0.80+ is exceptional.

:::

### Hardware: one small GPU

For this test, the hardware used was a laptop with 8 cores, 16 threads, 30 GiB of RAM, and a **small 6 GiB GPU**.

### Load packages

```{.python}
import json
import re

import numpy as np
# https://github.com/ollama/ollama-python
import ollama
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model, prepare_model_for_kbit_training
# https://github.com/dorianbrown/rank_bm25
from rank_bm25 import BM25Okapi
from torch.utils.data import Dataset
from transformers import (
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    AutoTokenizer,
    BitsAndBytesConfig,
    Trainer,
    TrainingArguments,
)
```

### Load corpus

```{.python}
corpus = {}  # doc id -> {"title": ..., "text": ...}

with open("scifact" / "corpus.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        doc = json.loads(line)
        corpus[doc["_id"]] = {
            "title": doc.get("title") or "",
            "text": doc["text"],
        }
```

### Load queries

```{.python}
queries = {}  # query id -> text

with open("scifact" / "queries.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for line in f:
        q = json.loads(line)
        queries[q["_id"]] = q["text"]
```

### Load relevance judgments

```{.python}
qrels = {}  # query id -> {doc id: relevance}

with open("scifact" / "qrels" / "test.tsv", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    next(f)
    for line in f:
        qid, did, score = line.split("\t")
        qrels.setdefault(qid, {})[did.strip()] = int(score)
```

## Lexical ranking algorithm

### BM25

A [bag-of-words](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bag-of-words_model) retrieval function ranks documents by how relevant they are to a search query. It uses literal keyword matches (1994).

Improved version of [term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tf–idf) with length normalization.

No training, CPU-based, still widely used (e.g. [Elasticsearch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elasticsearch)).

:::{.note}

Fails on [vocabulary mismatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocabulary_mismatch) & paraphrase.

Example: "heart attack" does not match "myocardial infarction".

:::

### Code

```{.python}
def tokenize(text):
    """Crude but sufficient: lowercase alphanumeric tokens."""
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())

# Build the index
bm25 = BM25Okapi([tokenize(full_text[d]) for d in docs])

# Score every document
scores = bm25.get_scores(tokenize(query))

# Sort
ranking = [docs[i] for i in np.argsort(-scores)]
```

### Result

```
BM25  nDCG@10 0.652  (15.0 ms/query)
```

:::{.emph}

0.652 with zero training, one second of indexing & 15 ms per query.

:::

A very serious baseline on this dataset.

## Dense retrieval

### The idea

A trained [embedding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embedding_(machine_learning)) model maps texts to vectors based on meaning:

- Index: embed every abstract once,
- Search: embed the query, rank by [cosine similarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosine_similarity),
- Solves vocabulary mismatch: "heart attack" & "myocardial infarction" have close vectors.

:::{.note}

Dense retrieval does not scan text; it compares coordinates. That is why it needs an index of embeddings.

:::

### 3 model sizes

| Model             | Params | Year | Disk   |
|-------------------|--------|------|--------|
| all-minilm        | 23M    | 2020 | 45 MB  |
| nomic-embed-text  | 137M   | 2024 | 274 MB |
| mxbai-embed-large | 335M   | 2024 | 669 MB |

Pulled by [ollama](https://ollama.com):

```{.bash}
ollama pull all-minilm nomic-embed-text mxbai-embed-large
```

Served locally:

```{.bash}
ollama serve
```

### Embedding the corpus

```{.python}
def embed(texts, model, batch=64):
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(texts), batch):
        out.extend(ollama.embed(model=model,
                                input=texts[i:i+batch])["embeddings"])
    emb = np.asarray(out, dtype=np.float32)
    # L2-normalization
    emb /= np.linalg.norm(emb, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # unit vectors
    return emb

doc_emb = embed([full_text[d] for d in docs], model)
```

L2-normalization makes every later dot product a cosine similarity.

:::{.note}

On the laptop GPU, indexing 5,183 abstracts took 150 s with the largest model.

:::

### Searching

```{.python}
q = np.asarray(
    ollama.embed(model=model, input=[query])["embeddings"][0],
    dtype=np.float32,
)
# L2-normalization
q /= np.linalg.norm(q)

ranking = [docs[i] for i in np.argsort(-(doc_emb @ q))]
```

One matrix-vector product against the whole corpus: [20 milliseconds]{.emph}.

:::{.inlinenote}

Each model gets its recommended query format \
Abstracts are truncated at each model's own context limit.

:::

### Results

```
all-minilm         nDCG@10 0.648  (20.1 ms/query)
nomic-embed-text   nDCG@10 0.703  (18.1 ms/query)
mxbai-embed-large  nDCG@10 0.741  (22.3 ms/query)
```

The 2020 miniature model ties BM25. The modern models do better.

Bigger embedding model → better rankings at [the same speed]{.emph}.

## Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)

### The idea

Fuse two rankings by rank position, no score calibration needed [@10.1145/1571941.1572114].

```{.python}
RRF_K = 60  # classic constant (Cormack et al. 2009)

def rrf(rankings):
    fused = {}
    for qid in eval_qids:
        scores = {}
        for ranking in rankings.values():
            for rank, d in enumerate(ranking[qid]):
                scores[d] = scores.get(d, 0.0) + 1.0 / (RRF_K + rank)
        fused[qid] = sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)
    return fused
```

### Results

```
RRF (nomic + BM25):   0.702 -> 0.706   # helped a little
RRF (mxbai + BM25):   0.741 -> 0.731   # hurt
```

Whether or not a hybrid method helps depends:

- With a mediocre embedder, fusion buys back what each method misses,
- Once one signal is much stronger, [fusing drags it down]{.emph}.

:::{.note}

Hybrid search is a patch for weak retrieval.

:::

## LLMs

### Commercial LLMs

It is cheap and easy to use a large, last-generation LLM running on the platform of a company (e.g. [GPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Products_and_applications_of_OpenAI#Text_generation), [Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_(language_model)), [Claude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_(AI))).

These models are now excellent at most tasks, including NLP ones.

There are many situations, however, in which they are not suitable:

- Reproducibility (companies can tweak, change, or take down models as they wish),
- Sensitive data,
- Concerns about bias in the models,
- Training on specific data.

### Open-weight models

Open-weight models offer a great alternative, but very large ones (e.g. [Kimi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimi_(AI)), [GLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLM_(AI)), [Llama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llama_(language_model))) require massive amounts of compute to run locally, fine-tune, or train.

Thankfully, small open-weight LLMs that run on a laptop can be powerful after fine-tuning.

Some open-source tools make this easy:

- [Ollama](https://github.com/ollama/ollama) to run them locally,
- [unsloth](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth) to train, fine-tune & serve them,
- [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang) to serve them in production.

We will use two very small versions of [Llama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llama_(language_model)).

### The constraint

A generative model [cannot scan 5,183 abstracts]{.emph}: it has no index & reads tokens one prompt at a time.

The standard pattern is [retrieve-then-rerank]{.emph}:

- Retrieve a shortlist: top-10 BM25 or top-10 dense (≤ 20 documents),
- Ask an LLM to reorder the shortlist,
- One LLM call per query: [extremely high compute demand]{.emph}.

### Naive prompt

```{.python}
resp = ollama.chat(
    model=model,
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a search reranker."},
        {"role": "user", "content":
            f"Query: {query}\n\nDocuments:\n{listing}\n\n"
            "Rank the documents by relevance to the query. "
            "Reply with the document numbers, most relevant first."},
    ],
    format=RERANK_FORMAT,   # JSON schema: {"ranking": [integers]}
    options={"temperature": 0, "num_predict": 200, "num_ctx": 16384},
)
```

:::{.inlinenote}

Full abstracts (median ~360 tokens), so the prompt needs a 16k-token context window.

:::

### Issues

Several replies per run could not be parsed:

```
query: 'The combination of H3K4me3 and H3K79me2 is found in
        quiescent hair follicle stem cells.'
response: '{ "ranking": [1, 3, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18,
            19, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 5, 7, 2, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5,
error: Expecting value: line 32 column 3 (char 168)
```

:::{.note}

The model counts & loops over numbers until the generation cap cuts the JSON mid-list: [9 of 50 replies unparseable]{.emph}.

:::

### The fallback hid the failures

The reply is text: code has to turn it into a ranking.

```{.python}
try:
    nums = json.loads(resp["message"]["content"])["ranking"]
    ranked = [shortlist[n - 1] for n in nums
              if 1 <= n <= len(shortlist)]
except (ValueError, KeyError, IndexError):
    ranked = shortlist   # fallback: keep the retriever order
```

:::{.note}

Every unparseable reply silently keeps the retriever's ranking: \
[the measured score was partly the retriever's work, not the LLM's]{.emph}.

:::

### Better prompt

State the number of documents, the valid range & the reply length.

```{.python}
resp = ollama.chat(
    model=model,
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a search reranker."},
        {"role": "user", "content":
            f"Query: {query}\n\nDocuments:\n{listing}\n\n"
            f"There are {len(shortlist)} documents, numbered "
            f"1 to {len(shortlist)}. Reply with the 10 most relevant "
            "document numbers, most relevant first."},
    ],
    format=RERANK_FORMAT,   # JSON schema: {"ranking": [integers]}
    options={"temperature": 0, "num_predict": 200, "num_ctx": 16384},
)
```

:::{.inlinenote}

All replies parsed.

:::

### New issues with 3B

Real reply to the better prompt, for a query whose gold document sat at position 1 of the shortlist:

```
shortlist: 20 docs | gold document at position 1

llama3.2 replied: { "ranking": [21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12] }
```

:::{.note}

21 does not even exist: the model counts down from N \
[The better prompt fixed the format, but not the judgment]{.emph}.

:::

### Results

```
llama3.2 3B   listwise rerank   nDCG@10 0.295  (5.1 s/query)
llama3.1 8B   listwise rerank   nDCG@10 0.557  (14.4 s/query)
```

:::{.note}

The 8B produces genuine orderings, \
but [both models still damage the 0.693 retrieval they rerank]{.emph}.

:::

### Good prompt

The listwise prompt asks the model to [do arithmetic over list positions]{.emph} — something small transformers are not good at.

Instead: judge one document at a time & read the answer from the model's own distribution.

### Score, do not generate

One small prompt per document, rather than a giant prompt per query:

```{.python}
resp = ollama.chat(
    model=model,
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a search reranker."},
        {"role": "user", "content":
            f"Claim: {query}\n\nAbstract: {full_text[d]}\n\n"
            "Is this abstract relevant to the claim? "
            "Answer with exactly one word: yes or no."},
    ],
    logprobs=True, top_logprobs=10,
    options={"temperature": 0, "num_predict": 1, "num_ctx": 2048},
)
```

### The score

```{.python}
lp = {e["token"]: e["logprob"]
      for e in resp["logprobs"][0]["top_logprobs"]}

yes = max(lp[t] for t in ("yes", "Yes", " yes"))
no  = max(lp[t] for t in ("no", "No", " no"))

score = np.exp(yes) / (np.exp(yes) + np.exp(no))  # P(yes)
```

Rank the shortlist by P(yes).

:::{.note}

P(yes) straight from the model's distribution: [no list to count, no text to parse]{.emph}.

:::

### Pointwise results

```
llama3.2 3B   pointwise  nDCG@10 0.668  (3.3 s/query)
llama3.1 8B   pointwise  nDCG@10 0.722  (7.6 s/query)
```

:::{.emph}

The 8B now beats the 0.693 retriever it starts from.

:::

### Fine-tuning

The LLMs we used are general-purpose chat models. While extremely large models are great at any task without fine-tuning, small ones are not. It is not surprising that they perform poorly here.

[Fine-tuning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine-tuning_(deep_learning)) can teach these models to perform much better at a narrow skill.

[Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)](https://huggingface.co/blog/peft) does this by only training a tiny fraction of the parameters while freezing the rest.

[Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LoRA_(machine_learning)) [@hu2021loralowrankadaptationlarge] is a popular [PEFT](https://huggingface.co/blog/peft) technique that trains tiny adapter matrices beside a frozen model.

Let's train the 4-bit llama3.2 3B that fits the 6 GiB GPU:

- [400 claims from the training split]{.emph} (the test split was never touched): the same `yes`/`no` prompt, gold abstracts & BM25 hard negatives,
- Loss on the answer token only,
- One epoch: [57 minutes on the laptop]{.emph}.

### How LoRA works

```{dot}
//| echo: false

// LoRA: a frozen weight matrix plus a trainable low-rank correction.
// Effective weights: W + (alpha/r) * B @ A
//
// Numbers are for one q_proj matrix of llama3.2 3B (3072 x 3072 ~ 9.4M
// weights; adapter pair 2 x 3072 x 16 = 98K). Across all 28 layers and the
// seven targeted projections: 24.3M of 3.2B parameters trainable (0.75%).
//
// Render: dot -Tsvg lora.gv -o lora.svg
digraph LoRA {
  rankdir=LR;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  nodesep=0.4;
  ranksep=0.7;
  node [fontname="Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif", fontsize=15,
        shape=box, style="rounded,filled", margin="0.16,0.09"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif", fontsize=12,
        color="#595959", penwidth=1.6, arrowsize=0.7];

  // Input and output
  x   [label="x", shape=circle, fillcolor="#ffffff", color="#595959",
       fontcolor="#30173d"];
  out [label="output", fillcolor="#ffffff", color="#595959",
       fontcolor="#30173d"];

  // Frozen path: the pre-trained weight matrix, never updated
  W [label="W\n3072 × 3072\nFrozen — never trained",
     fillcolor="#f2f2f2", color="#8c8c8c", fontcolor="#4d4d4d",
     style="rounded,filled,dashed"];

  // Trainable path: the LoRA adapters, the only weights that change
  A [label="A\n16 × 3072\nTrainable",
     fillcolor="#fce8e9", color="#b5111b", fontcolor="#8a0d15"];
  B [label="B\n3072 × 16\nTrainable",
     fillcolor="#fce8e9", color="#b5111b", fontcolor="#8a0d15"];

  // Sum of both paths
  add [label="+", shape=circle, fillcolor="#ffffff", color="#595959",
       fontcolor="#30173d"];

  x   -> W [color="#8c8c8c"];
  x   -> A [color="#b5111b"];
  A   -> B [color="#b5111b", label="r = 16", fontcolor="#8a0d15"];
  W   -> add [color="#8c8c8c"];
  B   -> add [color="#b5111b"];
  add -> out;

  label="Effective weights: W + B·A scaled by α/r = 2\n24.3M of 3.2B parameters trainable (0.75%)";
  labelloc=b;
  labelfontsize=13;
  labelfontname="Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif";
  fontcolor="#4d4d4d";
}
```

### The code

```{.python}
bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True,
                         bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct",
    quantization_config=bnb, device_map={"": 0})
model = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(model)
model = get_peft_model(model, LoraConfig(
    r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
                    "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"]))
```

### Results

```
llama3.2 3B + LoRA   pointwise  nDCG@10 0.739  (13.3 s/query)
```

:::{.emph}

Same 3B model:

Generating a ranking: 0.295 → Scoring: 0.668 → Fine-tuned: 0.739.

:::

:::{.note}

The judgment is calibrated too: gold at P(yes) 0.76 vs 0.47 for the next abstract \
The untuned model tied them at 0.82.

:::

## Verdict

### Full comparison

All the LLM methods run on 50 queries; the retrievers re-scored on the same 50:

| Method                        | nDCG@10 | Per query |
|-------------------------------|---------|-----------|
| llama3.2 3B + LoRA pointwise  | 0.739   | 13.3 s    |
| llama3.1 8B pointwise         | 0.722   | 7.6 s     |
| nomic-embed-text (retriever)  | 0.706   | 18 ms     |
| mxbai-embed-large (retriever) | 0.693   | 22 ms     |
| llama3.2 3B pointwise         | 0.668   | 3.3 s     |
| RRF hybrid (mxbai + BM25)     | 0.651   | —         |
| all-minilm (retriever)        | 0.622   | 20 ms     |
| BM25 (retriever)              | 0.606   | 15 ms     |
| llama3.1 8B listwise          | 0.557   | 14.4 s    |
| llama3.2 3B listwise          | 0.295   | 5.1 s [Fine-tuned 3B is now the best method]{.emph}.

### Best per era

| Era | Method                        | nDCG@10 | Per query |
|-----|-------------------------------|---------|-----------|
| 2   | BM25                          | 0.606   | 15 ms     |
| 3   | mxbai-embed-large (335M)      | 0.693   | 22 ms     |
| 4   | llama3.2 3B + LoRA pointwise  | 0.739   | 13.3 s:::{.inlinenote}

All on the same 50 queries, same benchmark, same hardware: a laptop with a 6 GiB GPU.

:::

### The LLM cost

|               | Embedding search | LLM reranking            |
|---------------|------------------|--------------------------|
| Per query     | 22 ms            | 3.3 s to 14.4 s          |
| Slowdown      | 1×               | [150× to 650×]{.emph}    |
| Model on disk | 669 MB           | 2.0 to 4.9 GB        :::{.note}

Only the 8B pointwise (7.6 s) & the fine-tuned 3B (13.3 s) beat the embedder. \
Fine-tuning of 3B took [one hour of training]{.emph} on the laptop.

:::

### Takeaways

- [Embeddings remain a practical and efficient choice for semantic search]{.emph}, and they scale gracefully: bigger models give better rankings at essentially the same speed,
- Hybrid fusion patches weak retrieval, but drags down strong retrieval,
- A prompted generative model is [not automatically better]{.emph}: asking it to generate a ranking was the worst method,
- Used right (scoring with its [probabilities]{.emph} instead of its prose), the 8B LLM beat the retriever it reranked on the same queries, but [345× slower]{.emph},
- [One hour of LoRA on the training split]{.emph} turned the 3B from the worst to the best method.

### Reach for the LLM when

The task is [generative]{.emph}:

- Summarize, answer, explain, discuss,
- Extract claims & entities.

:::{.note}

Retrieval and generation are different jobs. Let the embedder retrieve and the LLM do what only an LLM can do.

Or score with it when ranking quality matters more than speed.

:::
